title: Source and timing for every fact
current: "Visits record source/time; programme answers retain author and explicit absence values. Slice 2c: each measurement may carry its own source (measured or reported) and observation time, or a separate missing reason (not asked, declined, unknown, not applicable), checked on every save path and carried into FHIR observation times, methods and narratives; older visits fall back to the visit-level values. Slice 2g: the visit notes and each programme answer also record who recorded them (server identity and role at save time; older entries ""not recorded"") and a clinician verification state changed only by an appended, audited, scope-checked review on a confirmed visit; an owner can require supervisor sign-off before programme submissions are sent, recorded by a supervisor of the patient's team or a supervision delegate, bound to the visit's facts and answers so any later change makes it stale, and checked on the server before executePlan and again inside the delivery checkpoint; shown on the visit screen and the submissions view. Slice 6z: on a visit with no recorded entry or measurement author (recorded before slices 2e and 2g), the confirmer and, for a programme answer, the person who saved the answers are treated as authors, so they cannot verify their own entries; the person who saved the programme answers cannot sign the visit off. Slice 10g: a care-team member in normal scope (an ASHA only for an assigned patient) can raise a dispute on one confirmed measurement, the visit notes or one programme answer, with a reason and a reference; while it is open on a current visit, no programme plan or EHR publication that would carry the item is prepared, approved or run, the reason is shown, and the same check is repeated on a fresh read inside the delivery and publication checkpoint so a dispute raised between the checkpoint and the request stops the request and closes the item as not sent; a clinician in scope resolves it by appending evidence (closing it as standing needs a clinician who neither recorded the item nor raised the dispute), and the dispute and the original value stay on the record; a correction draft carries still-open disputes forward. An owner can set the sign-off requirement per programme and per destination (versioned with the organisation default, audited; a destination rule wins over programme rules, which win over the default, and the default covers programme destinations only), and a supervisor of the patient's team can withdraw a current sign-off with a reason, which holds sending until a supervisor signs the visit off again whatever the rules say. Nothing already sent is recalled; the screens say so."

acceptance: Acceptance: Each destination field can be traced to the confirmed source fact or a documented transformation; missing data is never converted to a negative finding.

title: Operational monitoring
current: Hourly request metrics, incidents, queue counts and cost assumptions. Slice 6g: versioned alert rules computed on each operations read, each with an owning role, count and next safe action, scoped to the viewer. Slice 6h: the owning role acknowledges an alert with a note; the acknowledgement lapses when the count changes or after 24 hours. Slice 5e: owner-owned AI budget alerts (80% and 100% of estimated monthly use) in alert rules 1.1.0. Slice 5h: alert rules 1.2.0 add owner-owned alerts for AI invoices of the previous month that differ from Saha's estimates beyond the owner's threshold, and for providers used that month without a recorded reconciliation. Slice 6v: each alert that opens is delivered in-app (top-bar bell with unread count) to the members who own it, from their own scope, with its delivery time; an acknowledgement clears it; an occurrence left unacknowledged past its severity threshold (critical 30 minutes, high 4 hours, normal 24 hours), or re-opened after its acknowledgement stopped applying, escalates once to owners inside the organisation with a recorded reason; evaluated idempotently on reads and organisation-wide writes. Slice 6z: an organisation acknowledgement clears only the notifications of recipients whose own view shows it (counts differ by care scope); the occurrence counts as acknowledged, and is not escalated, only when every recipient's view shows it; escalation notifications are written only with the guarded escalation update, and restore never re-opens a closed occurrence. Slice 10b: an owner keeps a recipient list of named organisation members (owners, administrators, supervisors) with a tier (1 to 3), a channel (SMS or email) and the alert kinds each receives, and sets the number of minutes (5 to 1440) after which an alert that is still unacknowledged is sent to the next tier. A demonstration simulator (mode demo; synthetic and training environments only, refused with 409 elsewhere) stores each message with a simulated delivery receipt and a hash-chained audit event in one commit, one message per alert occurrence, tier and recipient; recipients hold no phone number or address and nothing leaves Saha. Messages carry the alert title, severity, a count and a path link only, never a patient name or identifier (counts of care-scoped alerts are withheld from owners outside that scope). Escalation is evaluated inside the alert delivery evaluation (alert and Operations reads, organisation-wide commands), as a pure planner that a scheduled trigger can call; the owner screen on Organisation shows the list, open alerts with their tier schedule and the message log with lateness. Slice 10a: the same scheduled job evaluates every organisation's alerts and in-app delivery about every five minutes whether or not anyone uses Saha (at most 20 organisations, 800 database statements and 20 seconds a run; organisations with due work first, the rest in rotation), through the slice 6v writer, and records the evaluation time and counts in the organisation record with an audit event naming the scheduled job (first evaluation, on any change, and at least hourly); in-app only, nothing is sent outside Saha. Verified in contract tests and a local scheduled-handler check, not on Cloudflare. Slice 13d: the scheduled rotation continues from a stored cursor, and the job's records are written without moving the organisation revision (no conflict with a person's command).

title: Scale readiness
current: Slice 0a adds patient-partitioned loads and per-patient commit guards; slice 0b-2 scopes workspace reads to the viewer, so a local probe measured an ASHA read at 48 ms with 50,006 people (965 ms before). Slice 0b-3 pages non-ASHA scopes above 500 people: the same local probe measured a whole-team supervisor's paged workspace read at 34 ms and 5 KB, a 50-row list page at 38 ms and one patient's detail at 18 ms with 50,006 people, against 1.9 s and 38.6 MB for the unpaged read; search scans the scope (149 ms). Local machine only, not a reference device or hosted D1. Not scale evidence. Slice 6q: the patient-list cursor is opaque and name-free (`after:<id>`, resolved in the viewer's scope) and search text is sent in a POST body. Slice 0b-4: in a paged workspace, My work, follow-ups, the referral tracker and Submissions are built on the server over the whole scope (`GET /api/worklists`, one page per request, same order and counts as the unpaged workspace); on a shared local machine the work view took 557 ms and 11 KB at 20,006 people against 2.3 s and 18.1 MB for the full read, growing with the scope because each page orders the whole scope; the 50,006-person step stalled and was not measured. Slice 6w: work-list cursors carry the view's total as well as the offset; when the total has changed the server restarts at the first page and the panel replaces its rows instead of appending. Slice 13e: with audit indexes (migration 0017), 1,000 workspace loads took 23.8 s then 24.3 s over 4,000 loads (24.9 s then 32.1 s without them) in Miniflare; Worker memory growth is unchanged and remains open. Slice 14a (O-2): in Miniflare with an inspector, the application isolate's live heap after a full collection stayed at 11.55–11.61 MB over 3,000 workspace loads; resident memory grew to 551 MB without collections and fell to 322 MB after one, and levelled at 249–266 MB with a collection before each sample, so the growth is uncollected garbage and runtime memory, not an application leak; a one-file Worker using D1 grows the same way. Cloudflare isolate memory is still not measured.
